World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Rate rises, spending cuts and cost blowouts: Councils squeezed by fuel crisis
World.content:
Some South Australian ratepayers could soon be hit with rate increases above inflation as councils grapple with cost blowouts, spending cuts and project delays attributed to higher fuel prices.

With councils preparing their budgets for the next financial year, some are already reporting budget hits of $10,000 a week and potential project cost blowouts of up to 50 per cent — primarily due to the soaring cost of diesel and bitumen.

The state's peak local government body said while essential council services like rubbish collection have not been disrupted, the crisis may trigger discussions about cutting back on other services, increasing rates or taking on more debt.

Meanwhile, the state's civil contractors said there was now a "risk to any project" going over-budget, warning some businesses could go insolvent due to fixed-price contracts for public works.

Mount Barker District Council, one of Adelaide's fastest-growing local government areas, is considering delaying some of its road projects as it seeks more grant funding from the state and federal governments.

The cost of road projects, like in the Mount Barker District Council area, are "likely to increase". (ABC News)

A report published by the council last week found that the immediate budget impact of the fuel crisis was "likely to be in the range of $40,000 to $50,000 per month".

The supply of bitumen was also "uncertain beyond one month" according to the report.

"As a guide, some project costs are likely to increase by between 20 per cent and 50 per cent," the report stated, adding that a $2.25 million upgrade of Bollen Road in Mount Barker's west would be "subject to increases".

Phil Burton, Mount Barker's general manager for infrastructure and the environment, said the price of bitumen was having a "big impact" on road projects, including some that were yet to start.

"We probably can't commit longer term to those bitumen projects, and we're very cognisant about starting projects that we can't commit to finishing," he said.

Mr Burton said if the fuel crisis was prolonged, the hit to the council's budget could reach $500,000 a year, amounting to 1 per cent of its estimated $46 million in general rates revenue.

Phil Burton says the fuel problem is costing Mount Barker District Council about $40,000 to $50,000 each month. (ABC News)

He said the council was looking for "efficiencies" — which could include delaying projects "well into next year" — to keep rate increases consistent with the consumer price index (CPI).

"We'll absorb some of these costs for this current financial year," he said.

"The interesting discussion will be going into next year … and the pressures that will be on to meet the budget strategy that we have around rate increases being kept to CPI."

Contractors warn of blowout risk

Mr Burton said Mount Barker's capital works program was about $50 million and "we're expecting some of those projects to have an increase of 20 to 30 per cent on top of those costs".

"We'd like to see a pain share approach with the [state and federal] funding bodies," he said.

"We've written to the funding bodies saying, 'Is there any opportunity to provide additional funding to ensure these projects remain feasible?'

" Mount Barker's no orphan here. Every council's experiencing the same. "

Civil Contractors Federation SA chief executive Jess Tucker said the price of bitumen had risen as much as 40 per cent and said there was "a risk to any project across the board at the moment because of the rapid escalation of cost".

Jessica Tucker says rising bitumen cost could risk the completion of infrastructure projects. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

"If that continues, it's certainly not something that is sustainable," Ms Tucker told ABC News.

'We're going to have to cut our cloth'

Construction experts warn of mass lay-offs Contractors, business owners and economists warn that thousands of construction industry businesses could go bust.

Adelaide City Council is also feeling the pinch.

On Tuesday evening, city councillors are expected to discuss a rate increase of 5.6 per cent in its 2026/27 budget.

The council was previously looking at a 5.1 per cent increase but revised that up due to higher-than-anticipated inflation, according to a council budget report.

The previous modelling was based on the CPI being at 2.5 per cent in the next financial year.

It has since risen to 3.4 per cent.

The budget report floated "rationalising equipment usage" and reducing maintenance in "low visitation locations" to save money.

Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith said the council was working out "how we can shave some money off expenses across the board".

"We're going to have to cut our cloth properly because we understand we can't increase our income to cover the extra costs of everything we need to do," she said.

Jane Lomax-Smith says the council is looking at ways to reduce expenses. (ABC News)

Ms Lomax-Smith emphasised that no decisions had been made and council's "core business" must continue.

But she added that CPI had risen "higher than we expected" as had the cost of doing business.

"Nobody wants to impose unnecessary costs on any of our ratepayers, but we have to all recognise that the situation is remarkable," she said.

"We have to balance what we generate in income with what we spend on services, and that balancing act is something that has to be achieved every year.

"It's just more challenging this year."

The City of Adelaide typically passes its annual budget in June. Last year's budget also included a 5.6 per cent rate increase.

Rate hikes, service cuts or debt?

The fuel crisis is particularly acute for regional councils that have sprawling road networks to maintain.

Wakefield Regional Council in the South Australia's Yorke and Mid-North area covers nearly 3,500 square kilometres.

The council's capacity to provide community services and maintenance was "very dependent" on its vehicle and plant fleet, a council report published last month said.

"Cost and availability of fuel is also starting to impact on delivery of the capital works program, as costs increase and transportation of personnel and materials becomes more difficult," the report stated.

The City of Onkaparinga, Adelaide's largest metropolitan council which stretches from Coromandel Valley down to Sellicks Beach, said its long-term financial plan provided "little resilience to sustained global fuel market disruptions".

"If the current fuel crisis were to be sustained over the medium to long term, council may be required to consider difficult financial trade-offs," the council's agenda papers warned last week.

"These could include increasing rate revenue above CPI, increasing borrowings to maintain current service levels, or reducing service levels and capital delivery to manage cost pressures."

Moira Were, who is the acting president of the Local Government Association of SA. says councils are looking at a range of cost-saving measures. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Local Government Association of SA acting president Moira Were, who is also Mayor of Onkaparinga, said every council was looking at "any little efficiencies that we can make".

"In the city that's often easier, you can put your trucks all down one side to collect the bins," she said.

"In the regions, they've really got some challenges with the long distances between places.

" Every single council's having an increase, whether it's $4,000 a week, $5,000 a week, and so of course that builds up over time. "

Among the other options, Ms Were said, was reducing the frequency of council services.

"Something like an art gallery or a library, you might want to cut your hours back a little bit," she said.

"If it's about mowing the lawns and looking after your sporting clubs, it might be that you make them go a little bit longer instead of cutting them every week."

Ms Were said each of the state's 68 councils would make their own decisions on rate increases.

She added that waste collection was "not being impacted".

World.title: Mega theme park stalls as developer blames Iran war for alleged unpaid bills
World.content:
A $2.6 billion tourist attraction planned between Brisbane and the Sunshine Coast has stalled, with a company related to the developer facing legal action after allegedly failing to pay a local contractor.

But the company says the situation is being resolved and the project will still go ahead, as it blames payment delays on the ongoing war in Iran.

Infinity Planet, a proposed 68-hectare site at Elimbah, is to include a theme park, water park, five-star international hotel and a 9,000-seat city hall.

RHC City, founded by chief executive Ramin Ahmadi, submitted development plans to the City of Moreton Bay in November last year.

But an unpaid engineering report is threatening to derail the project.

The plan includes 50 cultural pavilions where countries can participate and present elements of their heritage and traditions. (Supplied: Infinity Planet)

QSHAC Pty Ltd, a separate company owned by Mr Ahmadi, contracted RMA Engineering for a crucial report required under the council's development approval process.

RMA says invoices worth $145,112 have been unpaid since October, with RHC City repeatedly promising to pay but failing to meet its own deadlines.

In emails seen by ABC News, the company blamed issues with the settlement of another property, and more recently, difficulties transferring funds from the Middle East.

Mr Ahmadi, who is Iranian-born, has been involved in dozens of developments across the Asia Pacific and Middle East regions, including the Tehran Mega Mall in Iran, which is said to be the world's largest shopping centre.

Ramin Ahmadi steered the construction of Iran's first large-scale retail and entertainment complex. (Supplied)

Part payment offered

RMA has withheld the final engineering report, which means the project cannot progress through council approvals unless the developer commissions a new report with a separate company.

In November, RHC City offered to pay $80,000 towards the debt in exchange for receiving the report, but RMA refused.

Will this $2.6b theme park proposal succeed? A mega theme park and entertainment precinct has been proposed for a rural township between Brisbane and the Sunshine Coast. But will this one happen?

In an email to RMA Engineering in February, an RHC City executive asked for more time.

"The project for Infinity Planet is currently at a critical stage. Our development application lodgement is dependent on your engineering report, and we have already processed the necessary council fees," he wrote.

"I fully recognise the importance of your work and the effort invested in this project.

"Settling your outstanding invoices is my immediate priority. I am currently working to secure these funds and request your continued patience for a short period longer so we can finalise payment and proceed with the next phase of the project."

The theme park site is surrounded by farmland and forestry. (Supplied: Infinity Planet)

After it says it provided multiple payment extensions, RMA Engineering filed winding-up proceedings against QSHAC.

A Supreme Court hearing was listed for tomorrow morning for the wind-up application, but after last-minute talks between the two parties, the matter has been adjourned for a week to allow for the resolution of the issue.

A spokesperson for RHC City's Infinity Planet told ABC News the "political and military" situation in the Middle East had made it "very difficult" to bring in the investment funding needed for the project.

"We are very confident this situation will be resolved in coming days and we can proceed with the development application," the spokesperson said.

"We are committed to creating a world-class leisure and entertainment precinct that will bring the world to Australia and Australia to the world.

" At times like this it is clear that there has never been a greater need for the harmony and understanding that Infinity Planet will create. "

World.title: Mother of Bondi Junction victim rebukes 'sympathy dressed up as action'
World.content:
The bereaved family of one of the Bondi Junction stabbing victims is urging the NSW government to address "what has actually been done" in the wake of the inquest and the attack's second anniversary.

In February, NSW State Coroner Magistrate Teresa O'Sullivan handed down her coronial inquest findings on the attack at Sydney's Bondi Junction Westfield on April 13, 2024.

There were 23 recommendations directed towards varying agencies and organisations.

Seven of the recommendations were given to the NSW government, excluding recommendations to NSW Ambulance.

Elizabeth Young, the mother of 47-year-old victim Jade Young, in late March contacted Premier Chris Minns, Health Minister Ryan Park and Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson for answers.

"What has the Minns Government actually done to implement the recommendations that belong to NSW?" she wrote.

"Not what has been acknowledged. Not what advice has been requested. Not what is being considered. What has actually been done."

The victims of the attack (clockwise from top left): Yixuan Cheng, Faraz Tahir, Jade Young, Pikria Darchia, Dawn Singleton and Ashlee Good were killed. ( )

A "floridly psychotic" Joel Cauchi murdered six people.

Elizabeth Young said families like hers did "not need more sympathy dressed up as action".

"Is this already slipping into the familiar void between portfolios, agencies and departments, where concern is expressed, responsibility is blurred, and nothing changes?" she said.

Jade's cousin Toby Halligan reiterated his family's focus on pursuing tangible change.

"They [the government] have not advanced on some of the really important things that the coroner raised," he told the ABC.

Toby Halligan wants to see progress on the coronial inquest's recommendations. ( )

The Young family received a response from Mr Minns after the ABC contacted the premier's office for comment on the matter.

"I can only begin to imagine the immense pain and grief that you and your family are experiencing, and I acknowledge your passionate advocacy for change that could prevent similar tragedies," Mr Minns wrote.

He pointed to a $111.8 million package from the state government to support community mental health.

"I acknowledge there is more to do, and the Government intends to do more," he said.

Mr Halligan said while grateful for a response, his family also felt "disappointed".

"My aunty was quite clear in her letter that she was not really seeking a [reply] acknowledging our grief and the tragedy, but that was actually being specific about what the government has done," he said.

"It looks to me like public service pabulum frankly."

The two-year anniversary was marked with a floral tribute at Bondi Junction Westfield. ( )

The NSW government is required to respond to inquest recommendations within six months of receiving them, and in this case has four months left after the February findings.

Ms Jackson said in a statement: "The NSW Government is carefully considering the findings handed down by the Coroner and assessing how they can be implemented to further strengthen our mental health system and improve community safety.

"We will never forget the heroism that no doubt saved countless lives."

Where progress stands on the recommendations specific to the NSW government

Recommendation 7 Recommendation seven is directed to the NSW government. ( ) Magistrate O'Sullivan stressed the need for short-term accommodation in Greater Sydney for those experiencing mental health issues and homelessness. She urged the state government to model, establish and support such services. Long-term accommodation solutions were also encouraged. While not exactly mirroring this specific recommendation, other housing initiatives have been invested in recently. Following the $111.8 million community mental health package announced after the April 2024 attack, all jurisdictional ministers for health and ministers for mental health across Australia signed onto an agreement — part of which focused on enhancing mental health housing. There has also been some investment in housing approaches such as Habilis, HAVEN and Pathways to Community Living. Recommendation 8 Recommendation eight is directed to the NSW government. ( ) With a deadline of 12 months for this recommendation, the coroner called for the NSW government to obtain advice from NSW Health on: The decline of and related demand for mental health outreach services in NSW.

The additional resources that are required to meet the need for outreach psychiatrist services for people with severe untreated mental illness.

The realistic time frame to achieve those additional resources and services.

What is required to provide a model to care for persons suffering from complex, severe mental illness.

A comprehensive report advising of options to improve the current public mental health system. Magistrate O'Sullivan called on NSW Health to ensure clinicians at community health centres have access to contemporary evidence based on "de-prescribing" guidelines, related to the potential risks if clients cease prescribed psychotropic medication. Two of the points in part addressed is related to outreach psychiatrist services, with funding for five outreach mental health housing liaison positions. Consideration continues on the rest. Recommendation 11 Recommendation 11 is directed to the NSW government. ( ) The NSW government was urged to consider options to support the rollout of appropriate co-responder models. This related to police officers working alongside specialised professionals — such as mental health clinicians — to respond to crises more effectively. In December 2025, the consultation period closed for a new model for responding to mental health emergencies in the community. It is now under review. Recommendation 12 Recommendation 12 is directed to the NSW government. ( ) Police regularly conduct 'wanding' operations in a bid to reduce knife crime in public spaces. It involves using handheld metal detectors to scan people. Given Cauchi's interest and use of knives, the coroner recommended the NSW government monitor and assess whether the current law related to wanding should apply to certain "crowded places" without the need for a declaration to be made. The NSW government has increased penalties for knife crime and increased NSW Police powers through a trial of wanding, which will end in December 2027. A statutory review of the trial remains underway. Recommendation 13 Recommendation 13 is directed to the NSW government. ( ) One of the most publicised recommendations was for the NSW government to promote how to survive armed offender scenarios. Magistrate O'Sullivan recommended an advertising campaign dubbed 'Escape. Hide. Tell', to be disseminated across the state, and for operators and owners of crowded locations to play their part. Consideration continues. Recommendation 18 Recommendation 18 is directed to the NSW government. ( ) The coroner asked the government to consider convening an urgent working group involving relevant representatives from the state's emergency services. The group was recommended to develop and implement an interoperability framework to provide clear structure for multi-agency responses to major incidents. Consideration continues. Recommendation 19 Recommendation 19 is directed to the NSW government. ( ) Last but not least, the NSW government was recommended that the urgent working group, as listed in recommendation 18, would consider the implementation of the 10-second triage. It is a rapid screening tool by emergency services in NSW. Consideration continues.

For Mr Halligan, the second anniversary of the attack is a deeply sensitive time.

"For our family it has had a catastrophic impact on us," he said.

"There is this preference for assuming that this is an individual monstrosity or an unavoidable tragedy and I don't think that's true.

"There were so many opportunities to stop this from happening."

World.title: Support service for Indigenous youth in watch houses to close over funding loss
World.content:
A frontline support service that helps Indigenous children held in Queensland watch houses will end this year due to a loss of state government funding.

The service, run by Murri Watch, helps support children and young First Nations people to ensure their hygiene, food, and medical needs are met while they are detained in watch houses.

The Brisbane-based not-for-profit's statewide youth cultural support program is set to end on June 30, following the completion of a funding contract with the LNP government.

Watch houses are used as short-term holding facilities for people who have been arrested and are being processed. (ABC News: Michael Atkin)

Murri Watch raised concerns that loss of the service would pose a significant risk to the safety and wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people.

In the last financial year, the charity supported 1,233 young people across 16 watch houses in the state, including in Brisbane, Caboolture, Southport, Mackay, Townsville, and Cairns.

The organisation's general manager, Kristy-Lee Costello, said its work was not an optional service as it supported children in the most vulnerable moments.

"Every day our teams are supporting children through crisis, often preventing escalation and keeping them safe," she said.

Watch houses are used as short-term holding facilities for people who have been arrested and are being processed, awaiting transfer to another centre or their first court appearance.

Murri Watch supported 1,233 young people across 16 watch houses in Queensland in the last financial year. (Supplied: Murri Watch)

A major review into the state's watch houses revealed adults were spending an average of 118 hours in them, while children were spending 161 hours.

"It is not uncommon for some stays to significantly exceed this average, for example, over 14 days," the review, released last year, said.

The review also noted First Nations people were disproportionately represented in the state's justice system and cited Murri Watch as a key service provider.

'Community-controlled approaches'

A spokesperson for the state's youth justice minister Laura Gerber said the government had delivered a record $560 million investment in early intervention and rehabilitation to restore safety.

In a statement, the spokesperson said the government was "making Queensland safer, with programs rolling out right across the state, including 22 First Nations-led organisations delivering 28 new services".

Laura Gerber says the government has delivered record investment in early intervention. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Queensland Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Child Protection Peak's (QATSICPP) deputy chief executive officer Murray Benton said Murri Watch played a critical role in supporting culturally grounded responses across the state's justice and policing systems.

"Their work remains central to community-controlled approaches that keep Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people safe when it matters most," he said.

Retired police liaison officer Uncle Adrian Coolwell said Murri Watch offered important services that took "a lot of weight off the general duties police".

"I know with the state of watch houses, at the moment, they're full and it's put more pressure back on them to look after people," he said.

Mr Coolwell, a proud First Nations man, worked for Queensland police for three decades and spent 14 years as the first assistant watch house officer in the state.

"A lot of people know the benefits of [Murri Watch]," he said.

The support service was established in 1991, just prior to the handing down of the recommendations arising from the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody.

Murri Watch, along with QATSICPP, is set to meet with the Queensland government this month to put their case a final time.

"We acknowledge and appreciate the Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support, and the minister for agreeing to meet with us," Ms Costello said.

World.title: Ex-One Nation candidate says Hanson must be 'held accountable' for rehiring rapist ex-staffer
World.content:
Two former One Nation candidates have accused party leader Pauline Hanson and chief of staff James Ashby of dismissing concerns raised internally about employing the convicted rapist and former campaign director Sean Black.

Robert Stuckey and Leigh Burns were chosen as One Nation candidates for the Western Sydney seats of Greenway and Chifley in last year's federal election and say they separately raised concerns about Black's criminal history.

In interviews with the ABC, both candidates said they left One Nation after feeling let down by the party leadership's defence of Black and disagreements over policy and campaign support.

"It's unforgivable. She [Hanson] has to be held accountable," Mr Stuckey said.

One Nation declined interview requests with Senator Hanson and Mr Ashby and declined to answer questions in writing.

Senator Hanson told Sky News on Sunday that Black had been sacked from the party after mounting scrutiny on his 2018 rape conviction was driven by the media, political opponents and "gutter politics".

"I don't condone this sort of behaviour whatsoever, and what happened. But he did his time, and he came out."

"I've had no concerns raised by the other female staff, no concerns by me whatsoever," Senator Hanson said.

Black was convicted of rape in 2018 but was rehired by One Nation before last year's federal election.

Sean Black was jailed for rape in 2018 and rehired by One Nation after serving his prison sentence. (AAP: Darren England, file photo)

Mr Stuckey and Ms Burns are now speaking out to draw attention to what they see as an inadequate response to their concerns as the party surges in popularity around the country.

"This is not about bringing down a party," Mr Stuckey said. "We believed in One Nation."

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, who was the MC at Black's wedding in 2010, before the allegations against him emerged, told the media on Monday that criminals deserve "redemption".

Both Mr Stuckey and Ms Burns agreed rehabilitation was important, but pointed to the judge's comments in Black's case that he showed no remorse.

"That really worries me," Mr Stuckey said. "It changed my view of One Nation completely. Not as bad blood, [it's] concern for the people that are hoping that One Nation could be a chance for a change to this country."

'Goes against every moral fibre in my body'

Mr Stuckey was competing against Attorney-General Michelle Rowland in Greenway, which stretches from Sydney's Blacktown to Box Hill, and said then-campaign director Damian Huxham initially assured him that his lack of political experience was not a problem.

When Mr Huxham abruptly left, Mr Stuckey said he called the national office and was connected with Black, who had a different communication style.

"I said, 'Mr Black, I need support with this area'. He said, 'Do you want to be babied?'"

Mr Stuckey said this abrasiveness caused him to Google Black and he found the ABC's report about the 2018 rape conviction.

Mr Stuckey, who has personal connections to domestic violence survivors, said he raised concerns with Senator Hanson directly on two occasions.

"I would happily swear on a Bible," he said. "The most concerning part for me was the lack of remorse."

Pauline Hanson on Sunday branded the scrutiny of Black "gutter politics". (ABC News: Matt Roberts, file photo)

During a campaign event, Mr Stuckey alleges he asked Senator Hanson if the ABC report was accurate.

"I thought, I'll go straight to the horse's mouth and say, 'Pauline, is this true?'"

"She said, 'Yes, but you know everyone deserves a second chance, he's done his time.'

"But that doesn't really cut it with me with certain types of crimes. There are certain crimes, like this crime, that are not something that can be swept under the carpet.

"My moral concern was that he was a convicted rapist.

"It could have been very simply handled by moving Sean … to a back room where he would advise, but not front and centre, not up front representing One Nation in such an open position."

Separately, Ms Burns said she tried to speak with Senator Hanson about Black but was told she was "too busy", so instead scheduled a call with chief of staff James Ashby.

The call took place on January 16, 2025, according to a text message seen by the ABC.

"I said to him, 'Look, the electorate I'll be working in has a high rate of DV [domestic violence], and I've just realised who Sean Black is'," Ms Burns told the ABC.

"He [Mr Ashby] was very polite but basically said, 'The guy's done his time. He's married now with two little kids.'"

Pauline Hanson with her chief of staff James Ashby. (ABC News: Jacob Kagi, file photo)

Ms Burns said his response was "flippant, dismissive and a bit of gaslighting".

"I sat with it for as long as I could, and then I just said, 'Enough, I can't do this.'"

Ms Burns said the experience had turned her away from politics altogether.

"It actually gave me a real eye-opener into the world of politics, and it's a world I just don't want to be a part of," she said.

"I feel unheard, unseen and definitely not listened to."

Both candidates' relationships with One Nation broke down over what Mr Stuckey described as Black's "aggressive" communication style and disagreements over policies and campaign management.

In one email dated March 18, 2025, Mr Stuckey accused Black of using "threats and intimidation, which only proves that this is the only way you can express yourself".

"I do hope that One Nation finally see that your methods are not conducive to developing strong relationships within the party and externally," Mr Stuckey wrote, copying longtime party donor and supporter Colin Fitzpatrick.

Do you know more? Contact Charlotte Grieve via charlotte.d.grieve@proton.me or Pat McGrath via pjmcgrath@protonmail.com

via or via If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

One Nation sent both candidates letters on March 13, 2025, pausing their campaigns "for one day, effective immediately, to allow for time for reflection" and demanded "full compliance with the party's campaign strategy".

The letters stated their social media accounts and campaign profiles would be hidden; they were banned from identifying as One Nation candidates until they agreed to use "solution-oriented communication" and "strict adherence to One Nation's policy platform".

"Personal grievances, internal disputes or attempts to challenge campaign direction will not be tolerated," Black wrote to Mr Stuckey.

"This matter is strictly confidential."

In a similar letter to Ms Burns, Black wrote that "party policy is final — candidates do not dictate policy" and threatened "immediate disendorsement" if five demands were not adopted, including that "all candidates must follow directives".

Ms Burns responded the same day, outlining problems she said she had experienced as a candidate.

"Some of these points would not sit well in the public arena," Ms Burns wrote.

"Just as your criminal history has not been well received by Women's advocate and domestic Violence groups [sic] that I have had the misfortune of having to contend with, which goes against every moral fibre in my body."

Ms Burns was disendorsed by One Nation, and while Mr Stuckey was permitted to stay on, he resigned.

In his parting letter, seen by the ABC, Mr Stuckey wrote that Black was a key reason he left.

"I was endorsed before finding out that yourself, a convicted criminal, was now running the National Campaign," he wrote.

"I have received correspondence from you wherein you referred to me as 'vile, contemptuous and evil … Therefore, I hereby tender my resignation for my candidacy, effective immediately."

Mr Stuckey said Senator Hanson called to try to persuade him to remain in the party, and he again complained about Black's criminal history.

"I cannot be comfortable going out and representing One Nation and having any one of my constituents coming up to me and asking, 'Why would you, how can you be against domestic violence and have a convicted rapist on your books? And I couldn't answer that."

Black (right) worked as an advisor to One Nation Senator Malcolm Roberts (left) before being jailed for rape. (AAP: Mick Tsikas, file photo)

After leaving One Nation, Mr Stuckey wrote about his concerns with Black in a social media post in April 2025.

"I asked with ALL of the crime against women, how could Pauline support this appointment, so it was a simple choice for me," he wrote. "If you are thinking of supporting One Nation in this election please check what [I] have said is true ABC One Nation report and then make up your mind."

Black did not respond to the ABC's request for comment.

Speaking with Sky News on Sunday night, Senator Hanson criticised a recent article in The Australian that published details from court documents in Black's rape case.

The article cited court documents detailing the offending and Black calling the victim a "stupid f***ing woman".

"You tried to push her outside where it was raining and kicked her in the shins, causing bruises and finger marks on her body and legs," one judge stated.

World.title: Feral cat numbers spark bounty push across outback Queensland
World.content:
Driving through the Queensland outback, something flashes across the headlights, but it's too quick to be a wallaby.

It's one of nearly a million feral cats thought to be roaming the state.

Two years on from a rat plague, feral cat populations have boomed across the north-west, leading more councils to adopt feral cat bounties.

But as council funds run thin, shires are calling on state and federal governments to help — an idea experts say will have little impact.

In the Richmond shire, about 400 kilometres east of Mount Isa, 6,000 cats were shot in just four months after a $10 bounty was introduced last August.

An endangered Julia Creek dunnart was found in the mouth of a feral cat in the Richmond Shire Council. (Supplied: Mathew Fontaine)

Mayor John Wharton said the pests were at historic levels.

"In previous years, we might have done a couple of thousand a year, but to do that in four months is unbelievable," he said.

Cr Wharton believed the bounty — which is fully funded by Richmond council — had been successful.

John Wharton says cat bounties have driven down feral cat numbers. (ABC Rural: Lucy Cooper)

"They're going backwards now. Don't tell me it doesn't work," he said.

"I'd like to see what the federal and state governments are proposing and see who's got the most [cats].

"Small animals and birds are being crucified in the bush … we've got to address the situation in a real, hands-on way."

Other councils follow suit

Cloncurry, Etheridge, Mount Isa and Boulia councils have followed suit, introducing bounty programs ranging from $10 to $25 a tail.

According to the Threatened Species Recovery Hub, feral cats kill 3.2 million mammals and 1.2 million birds across Australia each year and carry infectious diseases that affect humans and livestock.

The stomach contents of one feral cat shot in north Queensland as part of a coordinated threatened species program. (Supplied: Conservation Partners)

Macropod harvester Matt Fontaine is a professional kangaroo shooter based in Julia Creek, one of the last shires in the region without a bounty.

He said he had seen cats preying on endangered species such as the Julia Creek dunnart.

"I had my manager with me [and] we saw a cat with something in its mouth," Mr Fontaine said.

"It was a Julia Creek dunnart [in its mouth]. We were a few minutes too late."

Loading...

Mr Fontaine said in peak conditions he could spot 800 cats a night but, without a bounty, it was not viable to cull the pest.

"It's my job to go out and concentrate on kangaroos," he said.

"When I see there's other animals out there, I have to ignore it.

"It costs a lot of money in fuel to get out there, but then bullets, it works out to $2-$3 a shot."

Professional kangaroo shooter Matt Fontaine found an endangered Julia Creek dunnart in the mouth of a feral cat. (Supplied: Mathew Fontaine)

'If we lose them, then they're gone forever'

In 2024, the federal government introduced a national plan to stem cat-inflicted extinctions.

The plan prioritised species such as the night parrot and greater bilby and introduced policies to make pet desexing and micro-chipping more accessible.

Mount Isa councillor James Coghlan believed the approach had had little effect.

He said it was an unreasonable burden for councils to control and fund a national issue.

James Coghlan wants to see state and federal governments share the responsibility of feral animals with regional councils. (ABC)

"It needs to be federally coordinated and run by the councils and enough finance to do that, because councils are doing it all themselves at the moment.

"I've never seen tourists come to look at feral cats, but I've seen plenty who come … to look at native wildlife."

A spokesperson for Queensland Primary industries Minister Tony Perrett would not confirm if a state-funded bounty was being seriously looked at, but said "all options are on the table".

A federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water spokesperson said bounties were not the solution.

"The impacts of feral cats are so significant and widespread, we need to be strategic and focus our efforts on reducing their impacts on species and places that are most at risk, not just their numbers, which is the focus of bounties," the spokesperson said.

Threatened Species Commissioner Fiona Fraser said instead of funding local government programs, the federal government invested heavily in the Saving Native Species and Natural Heritage Trust programs to protect vulnerable species.

Experts question effectiveness

A 2016 report from the Natural Resource Commission and 2017 study by The Wildlife Society found bounties had negligible impacts on total feral numbers.

Charles Darwin University ecologist and Biodiversity Council Australia member John Woinarski said historically, bounties had not worked.

John Woinarski says feral animal bounties have not worked in the past. (Supplied: Biodiversity Council of Australia)

"Feral cat numbers are likely to be very high in western and central Queensland at the moment on account of some wetter years, and cats will be taking a large toll on native wildlife," Professor Woinarski said.

"Recreational hunting could play a role in reducing cat impacts under the right circumstances.

"Feral cat shooting is not coordinated, intensive or sustained enough to improve outcomes for wildlife — and simply paying a bounty won't change that."

World.title: As the Sussexes return to Australia, 'unusual' commercial engagements are raising eyebrows
World.content:
The last time the Sussexes visited Australia in 2018, they were newly married, popular, and still well within the royal fold.

None of those things are true anymore.

Even so, this still looks very much like a royal visit — although officially, it very much is not.

Harry and Meghan will be travelling under their titles of Duke and Duchess of Sussex, and spending much of the week making the rounds of various charities and causes they have aligned themselves with.

The well-received 2018 trip took place just after the couple announced they were expecting their first child. (AAP: William West)

It begins today at Melbourne's Royal Children's Hospital, followed by a visit to a women's homeless and family violence shelter by the duchess, then an event this evening with the families of war veterans.

Tomorrow, Harry will appear at a Movember event at Melbourne's Whitten Oval, alongside players from the Western Bulldogs AFL team, before flying to Canberra for events at the Australian War Memorial — where he will meet with Indigenous veterans, and attend a Last Post Ceremony.

A lot has changed since Prince Harry greeted crowds in Australia in 2018. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

On Thursday, they will be in Melbourne again, attending Indigenous and mental health events, before heading to Sydney on Friday to promote Invictus Australia, the veterans' charity he founded.

But there are some significant differences to a standard royal tour — most notably, the commercial aspect.

According to a media statement issued before their arrival in Australia, the Sussexes' program "will focus on mental health, community resilience, and support for veterans and their families, alongside private meetings and special projects".

Those "private meetings and special projects" include two major, ticketed events.

Harry will deliver a speech at a conference in Melbourne on Thursday, while Meghan is the star attraction at a luxury wellness event at Coogee Beach in Sydney next weekend.

The couple's day-to-day schedule will differ considerably from their official royal tour seven years ago. (AAP: Darren England)

According to the media statement, the Sussexes have included private events "to support broader commercial, charitable, and community objectives".

"These are separate from the core programme of public-facing visits."

So is it a publicity tour?

The media statement also poses, and responds, to that question like this:

"The programme is rooted in long-standing areas of work for the Duke and Duchess, with a clear focus on amplifying organisations delivering measurable impact. The visit prioritises listening, learning and supporting communities rather than promotion."

Excitement likely to be dulled around 'quasi-royal tour'

Royal expert Giselle Bastin, from Flinders University, described the commercial aspect of the tour as "unusual" and said the royals would not be impressed that the Sussexes were "monetising their visit to Australia".

"The fact that they are not working royals and are staging this visit as a quasi-royal tour would leave the Windsors nonplussed," she said.

"I suspect there will be many Australians — who were once big fans of Harry and Meghan — who will now be more sceptical of their motives."

The royals together mid-2019 for the christening of Harry and Meghan's son, Archie. (@SussexRoyal: Chris Allerton, AP)

She said the level of excitement surrounding their 2018 visit was likely to be much more restrained during this one.

"Both Prince Harry and Meghan were greeted by many Australians with considerable excitement in 2018, but I suspect — while there will be many royal fans still thrilled to see the couple — there won't be as much excitement this time", she said.

"Since 2018, Harry and Meghan have ceased to be working royals, moved to California, and spent countless hours in media outlets expressing their dislike for the royal system, for particular royals, and for Britain and its tabloid culture of racism and sexism.

"They are thought to have cast a shadow over the final years of the late Queen Elizabeth II and the Duke of Edinburgh, and for this they have attracted the ire of many a royal enthusiast."

Royal enthusiasts may feel different about the visit this time around. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

In the UK, favourability trackers suggest just 31 per cent and 19 per cent of the public have a positive view of Harry and Meghan, respectively, with the couple's ratings only higher than disgraced Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor.

Dr Bastin said the pair's tour down under was being poorly perceived in the UK.

"The tabloid press is having its usual field day with the way the Sussexes have not 'read the room' with this visit, especially as it comes just before King Charles III is due to visit the USA for the 250th celebration of American Independence," she said.

The prince has long criticised the UK's tabloid press, telling a British court this year certain outlets had left him "paranoid beyond belief" while making his wife's life "an absolute misery".

World.title: 'Can't put a figure on it': Greyhound industry rejects $14m exit offer
World.content:
Tasmania's greyhound racing industry has rejected as inadequate the government's proposed $4.8 million in compensation for greyhound industry participants, ahead of this week's crucial Legislative Council vote to ban racing from June 2029.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff announced on Sunday that the compensation package would be funded in the coming state budget and would allow industry participants to "exit with dignity".

Jeremy Rockliff says three quarters of Tasmanians "want to see the industry phased out". (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Beyond the headline figure, there is very little detail publicly available about the package the government flagged last month.

The details will be outlined in amendments to the Greyhound Racing Legislation Amendments (Phasing Out Reform) Bill 2025 when it is debated in the upper house, which is expected to occur on Wednesday or Thursday.

Asked how the $4.8-million package would be divided, Mr Rockliff said Racing Integrity Commissioner Sean Carroll would consult with the industry "in a very methodical way that takes into account the industry's needs and individual circumstances, as well as investments that individuals have made".

But greyhound industry representatives argued that, based on comparisons with the transitional arrangements in New Zealand, which has legislated a ban, Tasmania's industry deserved annual compensation of $25 million over five years, or a total of $125 million.

The industry has pushed back on calls for it to be ended. (ABC News: Scout Wallen)

Greyhounds Tasmania public officer Claire Robins told reporters on Monday that $4.8 million for roughly 1,000 participants in the industry was "nowhere even close to where it would need to be".

"I'm not going to stand here in front of cameras and put a price on people's livelihoods and lives," she said.

"[But] the New Zealand model that they keep bringing up — their figure is well into the $100 million, and for them to turn around and offer us $4.8 million, that's a huge discrepancy."

Mr Rockliff explicitly ruled out increasing the package to $125 million.

"That will not be happening," he said.

"It'll be $4.8 million in the budget and we'll work with the industry."

Transition plan could take years to develop

Upper house Greens MP Cassy O'Connor said on Monday that compensation was only the beginning.

"There's a process here to follow through with the racing integrity commissioner, a closure plan, [and] consultation with industry participants.

"It's good to see the premier come out and say there's been funding allocated.

"But he knows, and the industry knows, there are conversations to be had about what that compensation might look like and the racing integrity commissioner is currently working to develop the structure around that compensation package."

Racing Integrity Commissioner Sean Carroll says compensation would be determined "in a very methodical way that takes into account the industry's needs". (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Mr Carroll told the Joint Standing Committee on Greyhound Racing Transition in February that it would take time to determine how the compensation package would work, informed by a feasibility study on the transition being conducted by TasRacing.

"It would be dangerous to actually lock in what any compensation plan may or may not look like right now, until we actually avail ourselves with all the evidence and impacted areas and parties that may be required to be addressed in any compensation plan," he said.

"That may take two, three years. I make no apology for that.

"The issue of compensation needs to be addressed in a manner that is well-researched … but what I don't want to occur is that we're retrofitting compensation plans four or five years down the track regarding this matter.

"The reality is that compensation will form part of the transition plan. What that looks like, I can't say at this stage."

The Tasmanian industry says it deserves annual compensation of $25 million over five years, or a total of $125 million. (ABC News: Richard Baines)

The parliamentary inquiry, chaired by Independent MP Kristie Johnston, found there was a strong case for a just and equitable compensation package for industry participants as part of any transition and closure plan, and that compensation may be required and funded at different stages of the transition.

Mr Rockliff said in March that details about the compensation framework would be included in the legislation to be voted on this week, and a funding package would be outlined in this year's budget, "supporting a careful and measured exit from greyhound racing in Tasmania."

The commissioner is developing the phase-out plan for the greyhound racing industry.

'No amount of money' can compensate

Ms Robins said the industry was "nervous but remaining optimistic" about the vote this week.

It is understood to be finely balanced in the upper house.

This was Supreme Caesar's final race before it died, earning $0 for its owner Animal welfare activists are concerned the "true breadth of racing-related deaths" in the greyhound industry are unknown.

"If the vote got through, it'd be devastating," Ms Robbins said.

Greyhound trainer Katrina Gregory told an industry press conference on Sunday that "no amount of money is going to compensate the participants as such, and it's going to run into the tens of millions".

"It's not just hundreds of thousands. People have put their lives into their properties, their lives into the animals, and no amount of money is going to compensate that," she said.

"You can't put a figure on it. You can't, because everybody's different.

"You've got your breeders, your welpers, you've got your rearers. Everybody individually has put … money and time into upgrading their properties, their kennels, etc."

Greyhound trainer Katrina Gregory says it will be "devastating" if the industry is phased out. (ABC News)

A media statement on behalf of three combined racing codes — thoroughbred, harness and greyhound — claimed that "many of those who support this ban see it as only the first step in banning all racing codes".

"The only political party that supported banning greyhound racing prior to the last election [was] the Greens. As their national policy platform makes clear, they will now push for banning all other codes," the statement said.

On Sunday Ms O'Connor said greyhound racing in Tasmania was a loss-making industry that was "heavily publicly subsidised, at a higher rate than any other state".

She estimated about $100 million would have been contributed by the state government by the time the Greyhound Racing Deed had ended in mid-2029.

The RSPCA'S Andrea Dawkins says the greyhound industry has been "on notice for over a decade now". (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Yesterday the RSPCA released an open letter signed by 1,000 prominent Tasmanians.

RSPCA chief executive Andrea Dawkins — a former Greens MP — said the organisation could have garnered many more names.

She said this week's vote could be a "unifying moment" and that the greyhound racing industry had been "on notice for over a decade now".

"There are always going to be two sides," she said.

"There are going to be some winners, there are going to be some losers this week.

"We understand that industry participants will be compensated through that package that was announced yesterday and we hope that the upper house members look deep into their hearts."

World.title: The Labor figures and government critics in early health board exit lounge
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service The Labor figures and government critics in early health board exit lounge Matt Dennien and James Hall April 14, 2026 — 6:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: further health board intrigue, an audit office check-in, job swappers’ mysterious and important work, and more. After closing the tent over the long weekend to gorge on chocolate eggs, Circus has returned for one last bite at another item in vast oversupply: state health service board changes. In particular, the second cohort of members across the 16 boards who went unmentioned by Health Minister Tim Nicholls: those whose 2028-ending terms were cut short. Former Queensland Labor minister Paul Lucas, Queensland Council of Social Service chief executive Aimee McVeigh, former Labor minister Linda Lavarch, and former Labor candidate Donisha Duff are among nine no longer on state health boards despite having had terms until 2028. Our sleuthing of the state of play, based on the gazetted appointments and reappointments, along with comparisons of the new and former board compositions, has delivered results.



Assuming all health service boards have updated their websites, which most – if not all – appeared to have, we’ve found nine people who’ve left early across six of the boards. It must be noted that, while the government does have new powers to push people without cause, such looming refresh can also be used as a tidy time to resign for various reasons. Case in point: former Metro North board member Adrian Carson, said to have tendered his resignation back in August, to take effect on April 1 alongside the rest of the class of 2026. But Carson isn’t the only early departure from Metro North. Joining him are former Labor minister Linda Lavarch, not shy social service peak chief Aimee McVeigh, and Shea Spierings.



Over the river at Metro South, former Labor candidate Donisha Duff is also gone, along with Gail Ker. Related Article Public service A deluge of doctors join state health boards. But who’s out, and why? Another former Labor minister, Paul Lucas, is off the South West health board, with Darren Brown off West Moreton, Karen Prentis no longer at Wide Bay and former long-term public servant Michael Hogan, who got his state start under the Beattie government, gone from the Gold Coast. The key remaining unanswered question, of course, is which of those were booted against their will (and without cause). While those reached by Circus politely declined to elaborate on the record, and Nicholls has refused to say if he’s used his shiny new powers, we do know some were sent letters giving them a matter of days to explain why they should be kept.



Happy Easter! The work is mysterious and important for Premier and Cabinet job swappers The Circus tent lit up with chatter on Thursday night when one of our ranks broke news of only the second shuffle-out of a department boss since Crisafulli and Co put its permanent post-election picks in place. Steve Minnikin’s department switched leaders last week. Matt Dennien Most notably, the explanation of a government spokesperson around the job-swapping of Customer Services head Chris Lamont with David Sinclair’s not-quite director-general implementation role in Premier and Cabinet.



In the government’s lingo, part of a “Senior Executive Mobility Arrangement”. In the words of one former senior public servant, “it’s a parking lot”. Circus is certainly not shooting down the value of a good secondment. Particularly in circumstances where someone (Sinclair) hasn’t been a director-general or someone (Lamont) is still relatively new to the state public service. Related Article Exclusive

Public service Top public servant ‘exchanged’ into ranks of another department But such arrangements, of course, are also of benefit to the government of the day, for whom reassignment can mean avoiding any pesky golden handshakes for various reasons and/or a neat way to retain people who could be useful elsewhere. Look no further than the only other director-general chair to have had multiple internally shifted occupants over at Youth Justice – still yet to appoint a permanent replacement for Bob (Job) Gee.



So, of course, the question of why has loomed large over last week’s activity. (A question ignored by the office of long-term MP but first-time minister Steve Minnikin.) The government spokesperson’s line only that Lamont had shifted to help deliver whole-of-government policy and economic priorities gave little away. An additional one in response to how long the exchange might last perhaps said more. In a phrase reminiscent of one delivered by the fictional Mark Scout of Severance fame, the spokesperson said: “The work is critical and will take as long as required”. Artificial intelligence, coming to help trim an annual report intro near you One responsibility of Lamont/Sinclair’s department is the government’s internal generative artificial intelligence tool, QChat.



Because, of course, the public sector is far from immune to the hype train of a technology whose workplace benefit is probably still fairly described as to-be-determined. Someone who is in the engine carriage of that train, it seems, is the state’s independent Information Commissioner, Joanne Kummrow. A self-described “QChatter” as they are (apparently) known. Information Commissioner Joanne Kummrow. Fronting a hearing of her parliamentary oversight committee late last month, Kummrow was lobbed a question from the government’s Thuringowa MP Natalie Marr, curious about how the office’s trial of the tech was going (while conceding she was still, for some reason, focused on working out the fax machine). Kummrow said that to regulate the space and support others, she felt it was important “we are kind of in the sandpit as well”. And by her own telling, Kummrow is all in.



Some members of staff with a curiosity had taken it up, and were finding “great benefits” from it preparing briefing notes for her. Editor's pick Exclusive

Public service Inside the human rights office planning day that left staff in tears When it comes to trimming down an initial 900-word forward for her annual report into something more concise, Kummrow herself has also found a use. “I am not on the payroll for the developers or the department, but I have to tell you that I am truly impressed by it,” she said. We sure hope not, and can assure Circus readers that any trimming back of this column is done by sheer brainpower alone. And with not a fax machine site.



Is AI replacing town planners at city hall? Speaking of the wonders of technology, Circus had heard rumblings a potential AI rollout at City Hall would come at the expense of workers in the Brisbane City Council’s town planning division. City Hall is safe from the AI revolution, for now. Matt Dennien A council spokeswoman told Circus no AI platform was currently being used and there was no plan being considered to replace staff with machines.

Queensland government The LNP vowed to cap its outlay on consultants to fund promises. It’s still spending Which, of course, can also give rise to actual, potential, or perceived competing interests. “It is not realistic to eliminate all conflicts – but it is essential to manage them well,” Toma wrote. World.content:
Walk for Truth NationalIndigenous The long march to heal a nation continues, this time to Canberra Tony Wright April 14, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

More than 840 long kilometres lie ahead as Indigenous leader Travis Lovett and thousands of determined walkers set off on Sunday to march from Melbourne to federal parliament in the cause of nationwide truth-telling about the colonisation of Australia. Travis Lovett at Dights Falls. Jason South More than 1100 people have already registered to follow Lovett on the first day of the trek as it wends its way from the steps of Victoria’s Parliament House through areas of significance to Aboriginal Australians around Melbourne. One of the first stops will be at Dights Falls near the junction of the Merri Creek and the Yarra River, the site of many thousands of years of gatherings, trading and ceremonies by the Wurundjeri people of the Kulin Nation. There, Wurundjeri elder and educator Uncle Bill Nicholson will speak to the crowd about his people’s history.



The walkers will continue to nearby Victoria Park for an evening ceremony organised by Lathan Lovett-Murray, former AFL footballer and great-grandson of pastor Sir Douglas Nicholls, who worked for decades in the interests of Aboriginal rights and recognition. On Monday, 170 children from several schools will gather at the Aboriginal Advancement League headquarters and adjoining Sir Douglas Nicholls Sporting Complex in Thornbury, where the Mayor of Darebin, Cr Emily Dimitriadis, will host an event before the walk continues. On Tuesday, Travis Lovett and his wife, Renata, will step out along the Hume Freeway to Wallan, a route considered too dangerous for a large group to tackle. However, thousands more walkers are expected to attend special events and join short sections as the route wends its way past Seymour and Nagambie to Shepparton and enters NSW at Albury, continuing via Walla Walla and Henty to Wagga Wagga, and rejoining the Hume Highway near Gundagai.



The entire trek will take 29 days. It will end at Parliament House in Canberra on May 27, the start of Reconciliation Week and the 59th anniversary of the 1967 referendum that changed the Constitution, enabling Aboriginal Australians to be counted as part of the nation’s population. There, Lovett plans to deliver to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese a letter signed by thousands of Australians that calls for the development of “an agreed truth about our history”. “Truth-telling is not about blame,” the letter says.



“It is about healing. It is about finally listening to those who have carried memory and hurt, culture and resistance, through invasion, frontier war, stolen children, stolen land, prisons and policies that have too often treated Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people as a problem to be managed rather than as sovereign peoples to be respected. Truth-telling is an act of respect and an act of national repair.” Lovett said the purpose was not to reignite debate about the failed referendum on an Indigenous Voice to parliament. Instead, it was simply a request that the prime minister continue to meet his pre-election promise to address the Uluru Statement from the Heart, which included a truth-telling process in partnership with Aboriginal Australia. It is Lovett’s second marathon walk in less than a year. He was the deputy chair of Victoria’s Yoorrook Justice Commission when he walked from Portland in Victoria’s far south-west to state parliament in Melbourne, joined on various stretches by almost 22,000 Victorians, last June.



It was part of the process that led to Victoria establishing the first treaty with Aboriginal Australians in the nation’s history. Now the executive director of the Centre for Truth Telling at the University of Melbourne, Lovett wants to take the effort nationwide. Loading “We will be visiting many sites of significance to our people during this walk, including old missionary stations, places where massacres occurred, and areas of importance to the relationship between Aboriginal and white Australians,” he said. At Gundagai, participants will honour the memory of two Wiradjuri men, known as Yarri and Jacky Jacky, who – among others of their people – rescued at least 69 white people from raging floodwaters in 1852, using traditional bark canoes.



“The walk may be literal, on the roads and tracks we travel as Walk For Truth,” Lovett said. “It is also moral and political, choosing to hear what is hard to hear, to sit with discomfort and to stay at the table long enough for something better to be born. Related Series

Indigenous justice A time for treaty “A nation that can tell the truth about itself is a nation strong enough to heal, to repair and to imagine a different future.” Details of the trek and invitations for walkers to register and supporters to sign the open letter to the prime minister are on a Walk for Truth website. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Oil price up, local shares to bounce back; US markets steady
World.content:
BusinessMarketsShares Oil price up, local shares to bounce back; US markets steady STAN CHOE April 14, 2026 — 5:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Oil prices are hovering just under $US100 ($141) per barrel but Australia’s sharemarket is expected to bounce back on opening after US stocks held steady overnight despite ceasefire talks failing to end the US and Israeli war with Iran. Hope remains on Wall Street that both sides can still avoid a worst-case scenario for the global economy, and U.S. stocks climbed on Monday. Wall Street’s moves were much more modest overall than the extreme swings that have hit financial markets since the war began in late February. AP That hope is underpinning Australian futures markets which at 5.50am AEST point to a rise of 1.37 per cent on opening. The market fell on Monday following a poor showing by tech stocks, and as investors reacted to news of the ceasefire’s failure. In the US overnight, the S&P 500 rose 0.6 per cent in late trading after erasing an earlier dip. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 102 points, or 0.2 per cent, with an hour remaining in trading, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.8 per cent higher.



Even in the oil market, where prices briefly jumped over $100 per barrel after 21 hours of ceasefire talks failed over the weekend to end the conflict, prices pared their leaps as the day progressed. And the moves were much more modest than the extreme swings that have hit financial markets since the war began in late February. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war Trump vows to hit Iran’s ships as deadline passes for Strait of Hormuz blockade After weekend talks failed, President Donald Trump announced a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a manoeuvre that raises the pressure on Iran by trying to prevent it from making money by selling oil. A blockade would keep even more oil off the global market, after prices already jumped for everyone worldwide because of Iran’s restrictions on traffic in the important strait. That narrow waterway is how much of the oil produced in the Persian Gulf area reaches customers worldwide. Iran responded by threatening all ports in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.



“Security in the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman is either for everyone or for NO ONE,” the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting reported Monday. “NO PORT in the region will be safe,” according to a statement from the Iranian military and the Revolutionary Guards. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose to $US99.35 per barrel and is well above its roughly $US70 price from before the war. But it remains below the $US119 peak it’s touched at times, when worries about the US-Iran war have been at their heights. It also pulled back from its nearly $US104 price reached earlier Monday morning. “Markets are taking some encouragement from the fact that the two sides are talking and that the broader ceasefire seems to be holding, for now,” according to Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. And, as with so many pronouncements made so far in the US-Iran war, much will depend on the details of the blockade and exactly what gets restricted. “Not all blockades are created the same,” said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.



Trump said Monday on his social media platform that “34 Ships went through the Strait of Hormuz yesterday, which is by far the highest number since this foolish closure began.” In the meantime, big U.S. companies are beginning to tell investors how much money they made during the first three months of the year. Strong reports could help make up for worries about the Strait of Hormuz on Wall Street because stock prices tend to follow the trend of corporate profits over the long term. Goldman Sachs, the investment bank, said it made $US5.63 billion in profit during the quarter, more than investors expected. But financial analysts pointed to some potentially concerning signals underneath the surface, including lower revenue from the trading of fixed income, commodities and currencies. Its stock fell 2.3 per cent. Big banks traditionally lead earnings reporting season each quarter, and Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America will all report later this week. So will Johnson & Johnson, Netflix and PepsiCo. Helping to lead Wall Street was Sandisk, which jumped 8.7 per cent after learning it will replace Atlassian Corporation in the Nasdaq 100 index before trading begins on April 20. It will get included in such funds that track the index as Invesco’s QQQ, which controls nearly $US395 billion in investments.



Oracle’s gain of 11.2 per cent was the biggest in the S&P 500, which helped it recover some of its sharp loss for the year so far on worries that it may be spending too much to build up its artificial-intelligence capabilities. Related Article Opinion

Inflation The US is dragging the world into turbulent economic waters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Different kinds of worries about AI have been hammering software companies, raising the risk that their businesses may become obsolete. They also rallied to recover some of their big recent losses. ServiceNow climbed 6.7 per cent to trim its loss for the year so far to 42.2 per cent, and AppLovin climbed 6.1 per cent to get its loss for 2026 down to 38.4 per cent. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury remained at 4.31 per cent, where it was late Friday. Yields have largely been on the rise since the war began because of worries about high oil prices and inflation. That in turn has sent up rates for mortgages, which has hurt the housing market. A report on Monday said that sales of previously occupied homes were weaker in March than economists expected.



In stock markets abroad, indexes fell across much of Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 0.9 per cent, and South Korea’s Kospi dropped 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s larger losses. “The outcome of the talks was not really what people were hoping for, that’s for certain,” Neil Newman, Managing Director, Head of Strategy at Astris Advisory Japan, said in Hong Kong about the U.S.-Iran negotiations. “As we stand here at the moment, it doesn’t look very nice. Certainly, the oil prices are a big concern.” With AP The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

Indigenous justice A time for treaty “A nation that can tell the truth about itself is a nation strong enough to heal, to repair and to imagine a different future.” Details of the trek and invitations for walkers to register and supporters to sign the open letter to the prime minister are on a Walk for Truth website.
